node.label: Linda K Kerber
node.date_label: Women of the Republic (1980) · “Separate Spheres, Female Worlds, Woman’s Place” (1988) · No Constitutional Right to Be Ladies (1998)
node.description: A historian of women, political ideas and citizenship in the United States. Her 1988 essay examines how a language used by historical actors became an interpretive device for historians: separate spheres can conceal changing relationships when treated as a fixed social map. In her published 2001 lecture she investigates how apparently protective exemptions and unequal obligations helped structure gendered citizenship. The entry keeps this historical analysis distinct from current legal advice and from claiming one uniform experience for all women.

node.scope_note: New identity is the Iowa historian Linda K. Kerber. Primary selected essay pages and published lecture passage support two scoped contributions; monographs unread. incident_edges.relationship: Examines how the separate-spheres metaphor shaped both historical prescriptions and historians’ accounts of women.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 9–11 and 38–39 read. The critique treats the metaphor as a historically located interpretive problem, not proof that women never faced exclusions or that spaces were never gendered.

incident_edges.relationship: Investigates gendered citizenship through unequal civic burdens, exemptions and authority.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary Kerber section of the Summer 2001 Bulletin talk, opening and the Reed/citizenship discussion. Robert Post’s separate introduction is not attributed to her. Historical legal examples are her account, not current-law certification.

incident_edges.relationship: As Soll explains, Rodgers points to Kerber’s social and cultural history as a resource for enlarging the study of republicanism beyond political language.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll2010,22/n6 attributes this methodological use to Rodgers1992,38,and jointly credits Rhys Isaac and Sean Wilentz. Their distinct work is not collapsed into Kerber’s or asserted as a shared school. Neither Rodgers’s original1992 ending nor the particular Kerber/Isaac/Wilentz works were freshly read; Soll does not identify individual work titles in this passage.

incident_edges.relationship: May credits Kerber’s women’s-history scholarship as an early research influence and uses republican motherhood to explain the older civic lineage of Cold War domestic ideals.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2025 retrospective names Kerber in a plural cohort and note 7 cites Women of the Republic (1980); own 2008 Homeward Bound p. 98 explicitly uses her argument on mothers as educators of citizens before distinguishing the space-age version. No 1980-to-1975 causal chronology, sole-source claim or formal mentorship inferred. Complete Kerber original and Homeward Bound endnote 28 remain unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Kerber’s survey to situate later doubts about separate-spheres language in women’s history.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Cott’s1997 note18 identifies Kerber’s1988 essay as summing up restiveness with separate-spheres rhetoric, within a retrospective reconsideration of categories and gender’s relations to class and race. Nancy Hewitt receives the more direct credit for renovating Cott’s view; that role is not assigned to Kerber. The1997 text is discontinuous, and the precise missing lead-in is not reconstructed.

incident_edges.relationship: Provides Kerber with an account of domesticity, gendered work and the emergence of feminist consciousness for her history of separate-spheres rhetoric.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Kerber’s1988 essay devotes a specific discussion to The Bonds of Womanhood, explaining its domesticity/feminism argument and its extension of Thompson’s task/time distinction to married women’s work. This is bounded analytical use rather than blanket endorsement or a formal mentoring claim. The reverse Kerber-to-Cott claim concerns the later1997 retrospective.

named_group_routes.relationship: Adapts Thompson’s distinction between task-oriented work and industrial time discipline to explain the gendering of household labor.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cott’s retrospective describes following Thompson’s distinction when studying married women’s continuing household work. Kerber independently identifies E. P. Thompson and the1967 essay in her discussion and note14. Cott’s reproduced name is truncated at a page gap; the specific concept and Kerber’s explicit citation identify E. P., not Dorothy Thompson. Thompson’s original essay remains unread.
